item.title: Language Diffusion Models are Associative Memories Capable of Retrieving Unseen Data
item.description: arXiv:2604.26841v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When do language diffusion models memorize their training data, and how to quantitatively assess their true generative regime? We address these questions by showing that Uniform-based Discrete Diffusion Models (UDDMs) fundamentally behave as Associative Memories (AMs) $\textit{with emergent creative capabilities}$. The core idea of an AM is to reliably recover stored data points as $\textit{memories}$ by establishing distinct basins of attraction around them. Historically, models like Hopfield networks use an explicit energy function to guarantee these stable attractors. We broaden this perspective by leveraging the observation that energy is not strictly necessary, as basins of attraction can also be formed via conditional likelihood maximization. By evaluating token recovery of $\textit{training}$ and $\textit{test}$ examples, we identify in UDDMs a sharp memorization-to-generalization transition governed by the size of the training dataset: as it increases, basins around training examples shrink and basins around unseen test examples expand, until both later converge to the same level. Crucially, we can detect this transition using only the conditional entropy of predicted token sequences: memorization is characterized by vanishing conditional entropy, while in the generalization regime the conditional entropy of most tokens remains finite. Thus, conditional entropy offers a practical probe for the memorization-to-generalization transition in deployed models.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Pham B. et al. Language Diffusion Models are Associative Memories Capable of Retrieving Unseen Data. In Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
item.dc:creator: Bao Pham, Mohammed J. Zaki, Luca Ambrogioni, Dmitry Krotov, Matteo Negri

item.title: Bayesian Quantum Thermometry of Ultracold Gases with Non-Equilibrium Single-Atom Probes
item.description: arXiv:2611.27584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precise thermometry is essential for experiments with ultracold quantum gases, but conventional techniques such as time-of-flight thermometry are destructive and lose sensitivity at low atomic densities. Quantum probes provide an alternative route by encoding temperature information in accessible internal degrees of freedom. Here, we implement Bayesian thermometry with non-equilibrium spin-based single-atom probes immersed in an ultracold atomic bath. Temperature-dependent spin-exchange collisions map the bath temperature onto the internal spin populations of the probe atoms. Measurements of these populations are then used to iteratively update a Bayesian temperature estimate. We connect the information gained at different measurement settings to the underlying spin dynamics, identifying intersections of temperature-dependent population trajectories as a source of thermometric ambiguity. Using the expected information gain to optimize measurement settings, we experimentally compare unoptimized, a priori optimized, and adaptively optimized protocols. Both optimized protocols accelerate convergence, with the adaptive protocol reducing the average number of measurements required to reach a prescribed precision by a factor of 2.5 compared with the unoptimized protocol. In the many-measurement regime, we further characterize the protocols through their asymptotic error scaling and the accumulation of Fisher information, while testing consistency with the expected Cram\'er-Rao bound (ECRB) and the Bernstein-von Mises theorem. These results connect the microscopic dynamics of a quantum probe to efficient measurement design and establish Bayesian spin thermometry as a practical approach for ultracold-gas experiments.
item.dc:creator: Julian Fe{\ss}, Luca Granert, Sabrina Burgardt, Silvia Hiebel, Alexander Guthmann, Mohammad Mehboudi, Mart\'i Perarnau-Llobet, Artur Widera

item.title: Analysis of polarization drift of optical signals over deployed aerial-inground fiber connections
item.description: arXiv:2607.07629v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Polarization measurements of a classical 1550-nm signal are collected and analyzed on 15-km hybrid aerial-inground fiber connections over 11 months. The spectral area and spectral moments of mHz-resolution Fast-Fourier-Transform (FFT) of these measurements are extracted, and related to temperature, humidity, wind speed, and time of day. Spectral area correlations show a strong diurnal structure: daytime maxima align with temperatures/wind speed peaks and humidity dips, with lower levels during the night. These diurnal patterns also show seasonality, with higher mean and variance in summer than winter. A random forest regressor is used to estimate FFT features from environmental measurements, informed by a theoretical model.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Aneesh Ramaswamy, Nageswara S. V. Rao, Joseph C. Chapman, and Muneer Alshowkan, "Analysis of polarization drift of optical signals over deployed aerial-inground fiber connections," Opt. Express 34, 42428-42440 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aneesh Ramaswamy, Nageswara S. V. Rao, Joseph C. Chapman, Muneer Alshowkan

item.title: Memory kernel and closure for systems driven by intermittent forcing with power-law waiting times
item.description: arXiv:2611.23092v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many systems are driven by an intermittent forcing that takes on a random value for a random time interval. For such renewal step noise, the master equation for the driven variable has a memory kernel whose coefficients are the totally time-ordered cumulants, or $G$-cumulants, of the noise. In the case of Poisson switching, these correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the jump distribution, and the kernel can be summed exactly. We derive an exact decomposition of these coefficients for any waiting-time distribution with independent amplitudes and durations, which separates the jump statistics from the renewal statistics. For power-law waiting-time densities, $\psi(\theta)\propto\theta^{-\mu}$ with $\mu>2$ (finite mean), a long time interval is most likely covered by a single epoch, and we prove that, as a result, the coefficients cross over at long lags, at all orders, from the Boolean cumulants to the ordinary moments of the jump law. The long-lag kernel thus becomes a superposition of the kernels of the frozen deterministic flows, weighted by $\xi^2p(\xi)$, and the corresponding master equation follows in closed form. For $2<\mu<3$, where the noise correlation time is infinite, the second-order closure retains a finite error even for slow dynamics, whereas the frozen-flow master equation yields the exact stationary mean in that limit. The telegraph process is the only renewal step noise for which the second-order closure is exact. An exactly solvable model with correlated additive and multiplicative noise confirms these predictions.
item.dc:creator: Marco Bianucci, Riccardo Mannella
